mainTopic: Proving that רבי עקיבא holds מוכר בעין יפה מוכר and the רבנן hold מוכר בעין רעה מוכר, from the משניות about selling a house and a field
overview: The גמרא asks whether the מחלוקת between רבי עקיבא and the רבנן about a path to a pit comes from a general rule: does a seller sell generously (מוכר בעין יפה מוכר) or stingily (מוכר בעין רעה מוכר)? It first tries to prove this from the house משנה, but both halves can be explained another way. The רישא may be about what each side would put up with. The סיפא may be about whether we follow the buyer's intention or the seller's. Next the גמרא turns to a second משנה, about selling a field, which repeats the same argument. It argues the repeat must teach the general rule. That proof is pushed off with a צריכותא: a house needs privacy, and a field is harmed by trampling. Finally, the last clause of the field משנה, about selling the pit to someone else, has no such separate reason. The גמרא concludes שמע מינה: רבי עקיבא holds a seller sells generously, and the רבנן hold he sells stingily. The amud ends as the גמרא begins to bring רב הונא's report of רב's ruling on the הלכה.

steps.title: The suggestion: generous seller vs. stingy seller
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא proposes that רבי עקיבא holds a seller sells generously and the רבנן hold he sells stingily. It adds that the famous general statement about רבי עקיבא's view is learned from this משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps רבי עקיבא holds that a seller sells generously, and the רבנן hold that a seller sells stingily. And the statement made elsewhere, 'רבי עקיבא follows his own reasoning, since he says a seller sells generously,' comes from here.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its suggestion: the argument in the משנה is really about one big rule, whether a seller sells generously or stingily.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the רישא, רבי עקיבא says the seller must buy a path to his pit. That means the path went along with the house he sold, because a generous seller gives everything he did not hold back. The רבנן say the seller kept the path, because a stingy seller gives only what he spelled out. The גמרא also suggests that the familiar line 'רבי עקיבא לטעמיה' is based on this משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: A seller sells with a 'good eye': generously, so anything he did not exclude is included in the sale
A seller sells with a 'bad eye': stingily, so anything he did not include stays his
Following his own reasoning, consistent with his view elsewhere
In general, elsewhere
From here

steps.confusionAlert: This is only a suggestion. In the next steps the גמרא will challenge it, so do not treat it as the final answer.

phrases.english: As Rabbi Akiva holds:
one who sells, sells with a generous eye,
and the Rabbis hold:
one who sells, sells with a stingy eye;
and also that which is said generally,
"Rabbi Akiva follows his own reasoning,
since he says one who sells, sells generously" –
comes from here.
phrases.notes: That general statement about רבי עקיבא is based on this very משנה.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא סָבַר: מוֹכֵר בְּעַיִן יָפָה מוֹכֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the suggestion begun just before this section ('shall we say they argue about this').
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Proposed: רבי עקיבא = seller sells generously; רבנן = seller sells stingily; the general statement about רבי עקיבא comes from this משנה.

steps.title: Rejecting the suggestion: they may be arguing only about this case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how we know this. Maybe the argument in the רישא is only about what a person would or would not accept in this specific situation.
steps.simpleTranslation: How do you know? Maybe רבי עקיבא holds that a person does not want to pay his money for a house and then have others walk all over it, and the רבנן hold that a person does not want to take money for his house and then have to fly through the air to reach his pit!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the suggestion. The רישא can be explained without any general rule about generous or stingy sellers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי עקיבא, the buyer of the house would never agree to the seller tramping through his property, so the seller has no path and must buy one. For the רבנן, the seller would never sell his house and leave himself with no way to reach his pit, so he surely kept a path. These are commonsense guesses about this one case, not a general rule about how sellers sell.

keyTerms.meaning: From where? How do you know?
Perhaps, maybe
And others will trample him (walk through his property)
And fly through the air

phrases.english: From where do you know this?
Perhaps Rabbi Akiva holds:
a person does not want to give his money
and then have others trample upon him,
phrases.notes: This is the buyer of the house, who does not want the seller walking through his property to reach the pit.

phrases.english: and the Rabbis hold:
a person does not want to take money
and then fly through the air!
phrases.notes: This is the seller, who would never leave himself with no way to reach his own pit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects step 1 by offering a case-specific explanation of the רישא.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof from the רישא only.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The רישא can be explained by what each side would or would not tolerate in this case, so no general rule about generous or stingy selling is needed.

steps.title: A new attempt to prove it from the סיפא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries to bring the proof from the second half of the משנה, where the seller keeps the house and sells the pit to someone else.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, prove it from the סיפא: if he sold the pits to someone else, רבי עקיבא says the buyer does not need to buy a path, and the חכמים say he does need to.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the רישא did not work, the גמרא now tries to prove the generous-or-stingy rule from the סיפא of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the seller keeps the house and sells only the pit. רבי עקיבא says the path comes with the pit, which fits a generous seller. The חכמים say the buyer must buy a path, which fits a stingy seller. The 'fly through the air' explanation from step 2 seems not to fit here, so this looks like a better proof.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, instead (moving to a new attempt)
The later clause of the משנה
To buy himself a path

phrases.english: Rather, prove it from the last clause –
if he sold them to another,
phrases.notes: 'Them' means the pit and the cistern; the seller keeps the house.

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva says:
he does not need to buy himself a path,
and the Sages say: he does need to.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the רישא proof was rejected in step 2, this tries the same proof from the סיפא.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי עקיבא holds מוכר בעין יפה מוכר and the רבנן hold מוכר בעין רעה מוכר.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The סיפא of the משנה: when the pit is sold to another, רבי עקיבא says no path needs to be bought and the חכמים say it does.

steps.title: Rejecting the סיפא proof: whose intention do we follow?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the argument may be about whether we follow the buyer's intention or the seller's, not about generous or stingy selling.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps this is what they argue about: רבי עקיבא holds that we follow the buyer's intention, and the רבנן hold that we follow the seller's intention!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof from the סיפא by offering a different reason for the argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי עקיבא may always follow the buyer's intention. In the רישא, the house buyer would not want people trampling his land. In the סיפא, the pit buyer would not pay for a pit he cannot reach. The רבנן may always follow the seller's intention. In the רישא, the seller would not cut himself off from his pit. In the סיפא, the seller would not let a stranger walk through his land. This explains both halves without the generous-or-stingy rule.

keyTerms.meaning: Following the intention or mindset (of someone)
The buyer
We go (we follow)
They argue, they disagree

steps.whatToRemember: Both attempts to prove from the house משנה that רבי עקיבא and the רבנן argue about מוכר בעין יפה versus מוכר בעין רעה are rejected. The רישא can be read as what each side would tolerate, and the סיפא as whose intention we follow, the buyer's or the seller's. The גמרא then turns to the field משנה, and step 10 finally accepts the proof from there.
steps.confusionAlert: Notice that רבי עקיבא's rulings switch between the two halves of the משנה (seller must buy a path; buyer need not). Following the buyer's intention explains both halves, because in each half he favors the side that bought.

phrases.english: Perhaps they disagree about this –
that Rabbi Akiva holds:
we follow the intention of the buyer;
and the Rabbis hold:
we follow the intention of the seller!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from the סיפא offered in step 3.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof from the סיפא, so neither half of the house משנה proves the generous-or-stingy rule. The rule itself is not rejected: the גמרא goes on to try the field משנה (steps 5–9) and proves it in step 10.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The argument can be explained as buyer's intention versus seller's intention, so it does not show that a seller sells generously or stingily.

steps.title: A new source: the משנה about selling a field
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a later משנה where רבי עקיבא and the חכמים argue about a pit, winepress and dovecote kept by the seller of a field.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the proof comes from this משנה: someone who sells a field has not sold the pit, the winepress or the dovecote, whether they are ruined or in use. The seller must buy himself a path to reach them. These are the words of רבי עקיבא. The חכמים say he does not need to.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the earlier source and quotes a different משנה. This step sets up the next move, where the גמרא will explain why this משנה proves its point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same argument we saw with a house, now applied to a field. רבי עקיבא says the seller must buy a path to the things he kept. The חכמים say he does not have to. The quote alone does not prove anything yet. The proof comes from the fact that the argument appears twice.

keyTerms.meaning: A pit or cistern for storing water
A winepress
A dovecote, a structure for raising doves
Ruined, no longer in use
In working order, being used
A path or right of way through the buyer's land

phrases.english: Rather, from this:

phrases.aramaic: לָא אֶת הַבּוֹר וְלֹא אֶת הַגַּת
phrases.english: [He has sold] neither the pit nor the winepress
nor the dovecote,
whether they are ruined or in use;
and he must buy himself a path,
phrases.notes: The 'he' is the seller. He kept the pit and needs a way through the buyer's field to get to it.

phrases.english: these are the words of Rabbi Akiva.
And the Sages say: he does not need to.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof from the second half of the house משנה was rejected in step 4, the גמרא turns to a different משנה.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי עקיבא holds a seller sells generously and the רבנן hold he sells stingily.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The later משנה about selling a field, which repeats the argument over buying a path.

steps.title: Why repeat the argument? It must teach generous versus stingy selling
steps.stepSummary: Since the house משנה already taught this argument, the field משנה would be extra unless it teaches the general principle about how a seller sells.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why do I need this too? Is it not teaching us that רבי עקיבא holds a seller sells generously, and the רבנן hold a seller sells stingily?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the proof. The argument is repeated, and the repetition must be there to teach the bigger principle.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We already know the argument from the house case. Repeating it for a field looks pointless. So the גמרא suggests the second משנה is teaching the underlying rule. רבי עקיבא holds the seller gave everything away generously, path included, so he must buy back a path. The רבנן hold he sold stingily and kept the path for himself.

keyTerms.meaning: Why do I need this as well? This asks why something is repeated.
With a generous eye: the seller gives the buyer the fullest version of what he sold.
With a stingy eye: the seller holds back whatever he did not clearly sell.
Is it not rather...? This introduces the conclusion the גמרא wants to draw.

phrases.english: Why do I need this as well?
phrases.notes: We already learned this exact argument in the משנה about selling a house.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא לָאו הָא קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן –
phrases.english: Rather, is it not teaching us this:
that Rabbi Akiva holds:
one who sells, sells generously,
and the Rabbis hold:
one who sells, sells stingily?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This explains how the משנה quoted in step 5 proves the claim, by pointing out that the argument appears twice.
steps.raayaObject: The generous or stingy selling argument between רבי עקיבא and the רבנן.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The fact that the field משנה repeats the house משנה. The repetition only makes sense if it teaches a general principle.

steps.title: Both cases are needed for their own reasons, house for privacy and field for trampling
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. The משנה may repeat the argument for a field only because a house and a field each have a separate reason, so the repetition does not prove the principle.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe the first משנה taught us about a house, and this one teaches us about a field, and both are needed. If we had only learned about a house, I would say the buyer objects because he wants privacy, but in a field I would say he does not mind. If we had only learned about a field, I would say the buyer objects because people walking through damage it, but in a house I would say he does not mind.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof. It shows that repeating the argument has a simple purpose: a house and a field each give a different reason for needing a path.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Repetition proves a hidden principle only if it has no other purpose. Here it does. In a house the buyer wants privacy. In a field, people walking on it damage the ground. Since neither case teaches the other, the משנה needs both. So the proof for generous versus stingy selling falls away again.

keyTerms.meaning: And it is necessary: both cases need to be taught, because neither one can be learned from the other.
Privacy
Trampling, the wear caused by people walking through
I would have said not: the mistaken conclusion we would reach without the second case.

steps.whatToRemember: The proof from repetition fails because of a צריכותא: a house is about privacy and a field is about trampling. Each case has its own reason, so repeating the argument does not show it is about generous or stingy selling.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the גמרא is saying the הלכה is different for a house and a field. The argument is the same in both. The point is only that we needed to hear it twice, because the reason is different in each case.

phrases.english: But perhaps it taught us a house,
and now it teaches us a field;
and both are necessary,
for if it had taught us only a house,
[I would say that is] because he wants privacy,
phrases.notes: The buyer of a house does not want the seller walking through his home. That is why a path must be bought.

phrases.english: but a field, I would say not;
and if it had taught us only a field,
[I would say that is] because trampling is harmful to it;
but a house, I would say not.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This rejects the proof from repetition in step 6 by giving a different reason for the repetition.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: It rejects the proof from the field משנה. It does not reject the possibility that רבי עקיבא and the רבנן really argue about generous or stingy selling.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed the repetition had no other purpose. But a house and a field each have their own reason, privacy and trampling, so each case is needed on its own.

steps.title: A new proof from the last clause of the field משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings the last clause of the field משנה: if the seller sold the pit and winepress to a different person, רבי עקיבא says that buyer does not need to buy a path, and the חכמים say he does.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the proof is from the last clause: If he sold them to another person, רבי עקיבא says the buyer does not need to buy himself a path, and the חכמים say he does need to.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the first half of the field משנה and quotes its last clause instead. This step lays out the case, and the next step explains why it proves the point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this case the seller keeps the field and sells only the pit and winepress to someone else. רבי עקיבא says the buyer gets a path to them without paying extra. The חכמים say the buyer must buy that path.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather. It drops the earlier attempt and starts a new one.
The last clause of a משנה
He sold them to a different person
To buy himself a path, meaning a right to walk through the seller's land

phrases.english: Rather, from the last clause:
If he sold them to another person,
phrases.notes: "Them" means the pit and the winepress. The seller keeps the field.

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva says:
He does not need to buy himself a path,
and the Sages say: He does need to.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 7 rejected the proof from the first half of the field משנה, this step tries again using the last clause of the same משנה.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי עקיבא holds a seller sells generously and the חכמים hold a seller sells stingily.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The last clause of the field משנה: a pit and winepress sold to another person.

steps.title: The repeated case must teach the general rule
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why we need the field case at all, since it is the same as the house case. It answers that the משנה must be teaching the general rule: רבי עקיבא says a seller sells generously, and the חכמים say a seller sells stingily.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why do I need this one too? It is the same as that one! Isn't it teaching us that רבי עקיבא holds a seller sells generously, and the חכמים hold a seller sells stingily?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the last clause is a proof. Selling to another person already appears in the house משנה, so repeating it for a field must be teaching something new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 7 the first half of the field משנה was explained away, because a house and a field could each have their own reason. In the case of selling to another person, the גמרא gives no such separate reason, so the repeat looks truly extra. The only good reason to repeat it is to teach a general rule about how every seller sells.

keyTerms.meaning: Why do I need this too? This asks why the text repeats itself.
This is the same as that
This is what it is teaching us
Generously, literally "with a good eye"
Stingily, literally "with a bad eye"

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix this up with step 7. There the repeat was explained by a separate reason for house and field. Here the גמרא gives no such reason, which is why the repeat now works as a proof.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the general principle about how a seller sells, and that principle can be used for many sales, not only houses and fields.

phrases.english: Why do I need this one too?
It is the same as that one!
phrases.notes: "That one" is the house משנה's case where the seller keeps the house and sells the pit to someone else.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא לָאו הָא קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן –
phrases.english: Rather, isn't it teaching us this:
that Rabbi Akiva holds:
a seller sells generously,
and the Rabbis hold:
a seller sells stingily?

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא תּוּ לְמָה לִי? הַיְינוּ הָךְ!
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the clause quoted in step 8 proves the point. The משנה repeats itself, so the repeat must be teaching something.
steps.raayaObject: The argument between רבי עקיבא and the חכמים is about a general rule: does a seller sell generously or stingily?
steps.raayaSupportSource: The extra repeat of the sell-to-another case in the field משנה, after the house משנה already taught it.

steps.title: The proof is accepted
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא agrees that the proof works: רבי עקיבא and the חכמים argue about whether a seller sells generously or stingily.
steps.simpleTranslation: Learn from this that it is so.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts the proof from step 9. This closes the search for a source that started back in the earlier steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier proofs were pushed away, but this one stands. It is now settled that the argument between רבי עקיבא and the חכמים is about how a seller sells in general.

keyTerms.meaning: Learn from it. The גמרא is saying the proof works.

steps.whatToRemember: רבי עקיבא: a seller sells generously (בעין יפה), so the path goes with whatever he sold. If he keeps the pit, he must buy a path. If he sells the pit, the buyer gets the path free. חכמים: a seller sells stingily (בעין רעה), so the path stays with the seller. If he keeps the pit, he needs no path. If he sells the pit, the buyer must buy one. This is proven from the extra repeat in the last clause of the field משנה.

phrases.english: Learn from this that it is so.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the proof made in step 9.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבי עקיבא holds מוכר בעין יפה מוכר, and the חכמים hold מוכר בעין רעה מוכר.

steps.title: Opening the discussion on what the law is
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא introduces a statement by the אמוראים about the final הלכה, beginning with what רב הונא said in the name of רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was said: רב הונא said in the name of רב:
steps.whatsHappening: This is only a setup line. The גמרא is about to tell us how רב decided the הלכה in this argument, and his actual words come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now that we know what the argument is about, the next question is whose view we follow. The word איתמר tells us that later Sages (אמוראים) argued about this question.

keyTerms.meaning: It was said. This introduces a statement or an argument between אמוראים.
An אמורא and a leading student of רב

phrases.english: It was said:
Rav Huna said in the name of Rav:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from proving what the argument is about to deciding what the law is.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Not stated yet. This line only introduces רב's ruling, which comes next.
